Chien-Shiung Wu The physicist who showed nature isn't left-right symmetric

For thirty years physicists assumed that nature could not tell left from right, and that any experiment, viewed in a mirror, would obey exactly the same laws. In the winter of 1956, working with cobalt-60 cooled to within a hundredth of a degree of absolute zero, Chien-Shiung Wu showed that this was false. The weak interaction, one of the four fundamental forces, behaves differently in a mirror. This museum has six rooms. Walk them in whatever order you like.

There is no set path through this museum. Every exhibit stands on its own, and each one has a Home button that brings you back here. Nothing is locked, and nothing has to be finished first.

Six rooms

Room 2 is the largest. It holds the experiment itself.

SELECT ANY ROOM TO ENTER

One sentence, if you only read one

Wu cooled a sample of radioactive cobalt-60 until its nuclei could be lined up by a magnetic field so they all spun the same way. She then counted the electrons thrown out by beta decay. If nature could not tell left from right, equal numbers should have come out along the spin and against it. Instead, noticeably more came out against the direction of the nuclear spin. The mirror image of her experiment is not something nature actually does, and that had never been seen before.

The weak interaction does not always behave the same way in a mirror image.
The finding this museum is built around
ROOM 01 · MEET THE PHYSICIST

Meet the Physicist

Chien-Shiung Wu (吳健雄) was a Chinese-American experimental and nuclear physicist. She was born on 31 May 1912 in Liuhe, near Shanghai, and died on 16 February 1997 in New York City (National Park Service, n.d.). Colleagues called her the First Lady of Physics. She spent her career designing the kind of careful, difficult measurements that decide which theories survive.

What she looked like

Four photographs from the Smithsonian's Science Service collection. Select any image to enlarge it. The credit for each one sits directly underneath.

Why an experimentalist matters

Physics runs on two kinds of people. Theorists propose how nature might work. Experimentalists find out whether it actually does. Wu was one of the finest experimentalists of her generation: she was known for choosing the measurement that would settle an argument, and for being ruthless about sources of error.

Before the parity work she had already made her name by producing the cleanest measurements of beta-decay energy spectra anyone had managed, which supported Enrico Fermi's 1933 theory of beta decay. That reputation is exactly why Lee and Yang came to her in 1956.

A life, opened out

Select any year to read what happened. You can have several open at once.

Wu was born in the small town of Liuhe in Taicang, Jiangsu province. Her father, Wu Zhong-Yi, had founded a school for girls in the town, an unusual thing in China at the time, and she was among its first students (National Park Service, 2022). Her family's belief that girls should be educated shaped the whole course of her life.

Wu graduated at the top of her class with a bachelor's degree in physics (Angelucci, 2021). She then spent time working in a physics laboratory and teaching before deciding to continue her training abroad, since China at the time had very limited facilities for graduate work in experimental physics.

Wu left China by ship, intending to study at the University of Michigan. During a stop in San Francisco she visited the University of California, Berkeley, saw its radiation laboratory, and changed her plans (National Park Service, 2022). She never returned to live in China; the Second World War and then the political situation kept her away, and she did not see her family again.

Wu completed her doctorate at Berkeley, where the physics department included Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, and Emilio Segrè. Her doctoral research dealt with the products of uranium fission and with beta decay, the two subjects that would define her career. Despite an outstanding record, she was not offered a faculty position at a major research university at the time (Angelucci, 2021).

Wu married the physicist Luke Chia-Liu Yuan in 1942 and moved east. She taught first at Smith College, a women's college, then was hired at Princeton University as the first woman appointed to the faculty of its physics department, at a time when Princeton's undergraduate student body was entirely male (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, n.d.).

Wu joined Columbia's Substitute Alloy Materials Laboratories, the division of the Manhattan Project based there. Her work involved improving radiation detectors and contributing to the gaseous-diffusion process used to separate uranium isotopes. Her earlier research on fission products also proved directly useful when a reactor at Hanford kept shutting itself down (National Park Service, n.d.).

Wu was promoted to associate professor in 1952 and to full professor in 1958, becoming the first woman to hold a tenured position in Columbia's physics department. In 1958 she was also elected to the United States National Academy of Sciences (Angelucci, 2021).

In the summer of 1956, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang asked Wu whether the assumption that parity is conserved had ever actually been tested for the weak interaction. Wu cancelled a planned trip abroad and began work. Together with the low-temperature group at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington (Ernest Ambler, Raymond Hayward, Dale Hoppes and Ralph Hudson), she built an apparatus that could align cobalt-60 nuclei near absolute zero. The result arrived at the end of December 1956 and was published in Physical Review in February 1957 (Wu et al., 1957). Room 02 covers this in full.

Wu received the National Academy of Sciences' Comstock Prize in Physics in 1964, the National Medal of Science in 1975, and the first Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978. In 1973 she was named the first Michael I. Pupin Professor of Physics at Columbia. She was also elected the first woman president of the American Physical Society, in 1975 (Angelucci, 2021).

Wu retired from Columbia in 1981 and spent her later years lecturing, campaigning for girls and women to be encouraged into science, and supporting science education in China and Taiwan. She died in New York City on 16 February 1997, aged 84 (National Park Service, 2022).

Education and career, side by side

Where she trained, and what she did with it.

Wartime work at Columbia

From 1944 she worked in Columbia's Substitute Alloy Materials Laboratories on the Manhattan Project. Two concrete contributions: better radiation detectors for measuring radioactivity accurately, and work on the gaseous-diffusion method of separating uranium isotopes, the process that concentrates uranium-235 out of natural uranium (National Park Service, n.d.).

A career built on beta decay

Wu returned to beta decay after the war and became the leading experimental authority on it. Her measurements supported Fermi's theory of beta decay, her cobalt-60 experiment of 1956 and 1957 overturned the assumption of parity conservation, and her 1965 textbook Beta Decay remained a standard reference for decades (Atomic Heritage Foundation, n.d.).

1912 to 1997Liuhe, China → New York City
1940PhD, UC Berkeley
1943First woman on Princeton's physics faculty
1975First woman president of the American Physical Society

Did you know?

Three things about Wu that don't usually make it into the one-paragraph version.

The first large plutonium-production reactor at Hanford started up in 1944 and then shut itself down, repeatedly, for no obvious reason. Enrico Fermi and his colleagues worked out that a fission product was absorbing neutrons and poisoning the chain reaction. Wu's unpublished doctoral work at Berkeley had dealt with exactly this material, the xenon isotope responsible, and her results helped confirm the explanation (National Park Service, n.d.).

Wu left China intending to come back after her doctorate. The Second World War in the Pacific, then the political division that followed, made return impossible. She was not able to visit China again until 1973, by which time her parents had died. Her wedding in 1942 was attended by neither family.

Wu had been a full professor at Columbia since 1958 and the holder of a named chair since 1973. Her salary was brought into line with that of her male colleagues of equivalent rank in 1975, seventeen years after her promotion to full professor (National Park Service, 2022).

ROOM 02 · MAIN HALL · SHOW ME THE PHYSICS

Show Me the Physics

This room holds the experiment. Start anywhere: read the problem, pull the apparatus apart, flip the whole thing into a mirror, or jump to the quiz at the end. Everything here is built on the paper Wu and her collaborators published in Physical Review in February 1957.

The problem, in plain language

Parity is a type of symmetry. It asks whether the laws of physics behave the same way when a physical situation is compared with its mirror image. Take any experiment, build the exact mirror-reversed version of it, and run it. If the mirror version is something nature can also do, and it happens just as often, parity is conserved.

By the 1950s parity conservation had been carefully checked for the electromagnetic force and for the strong nuclear force. It held. Physicists assumed it held everywhere, including for the weak interaction, the force responsible for beta decay. It turned out that nobody had actually checked.

The τ-θ puzzle

What forced the question was an awkward result in particle physics. Two particles, then called tau and theta, appeared to be identical in mass and lifetime, but one decayed into a two-particle state and the other into a three-particle state, and those two states have opposite parity. Either they were two different particles that were suspiciously alike, or they were one particle and parity was not conserved in its decay.

Lee and Yang ask the question

In 1956 two theorists at Columbia and Princeton, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang, reviewed the entire experimental literature. Their conclusion was sharp: for the weak interaction, the data neither confirmed nor refuted parity conservation. It had simply been assumed. They proposed several experiments that could settle it. Most physicists thought the effort was not worth it (Lee & Yang, 1956). Wu disagreed.

Take the apparatus apart

Select any labelled part of the rig, or use the buttons underneath, to read what it did and why it had to be there.

SCHEMATIC · DRAWN FOR THIS EXHIBIT, NOT TO SCALE

SELECT A PART

Six things had to work at once

Wu's problem was not conceptual. Lee and Yang had already said what to look for. Her problem was that the measurement demanded a radioactive source, a magnetic field, a temperature near absolute zero, and a particle counter, all in the same apparatus, all behaving well at the same time. No single laboratory had that combination, which is why she took the experiment to the low-temperature group at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington.

Source · cobalt-60, a beta-minus emitter
Temperature · roughly 0.01 kelvin
Field · magnetic, to line the nuclei up
Measured · direction of emitted electrons

A note on the schematic above: it is simplified so that each part can be pointed at separately. In the real apparatus the cobalt-60 was a thin layer on the surface of a cerium magnesium nitrate crystal, the scintillator that counted the electrons sat inside the vacuum space above the source with its light carried out along a transparent rod, and two further detectors watched the gamma rays from the daughter nickel nuclei to confirm that the cobalt really was still lined up.

What is actually decaying

Cobalt-60 is unstable. It undergoes beta-minus decay, turning into nickel-60.

⁶⁰Co → ⁶⁰Ni + e⁻ + ν̄e A cobalt-60 nucleus becomes a nickel-60 nucleus, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. The nickel is left in an excited state and sheds the extra energy as gamma rays, which is how Wu's team checked that the cobalt nuclei were still properly lined up.

n → p + e⁻ + ν̄e Zoom in and this is what is happening inside the nucleus: a single neutron turns into a proton, throwing out an electron and an electron antineutrino. The number of nucleons stays at 60; the atomic number climbs from 27 to 28, which is why the element changes.

Why an antineutrino has to be there

Before the neutrino was proposed, beta decay looked broken. The emitted electrons came out with a whole range of energies instead of one fixed value, which appeared to violate conservation of energy. Adding a second, nearly undetectable particle that carries away the rest of the energy fixes the problem, and it also balances momentum and angular momentum. The particle emitted alongside the electron in beta-minus decay is the electron antineutrino.

The particles, one line each

nNeutron. A nucleon with no electric charge, found in the nucleus. In beta-minus decay it is the particle that changes.
pProton. A nucleon with charge +1e. Gaining one proton moves the atom one place up the periodic table: cobalt (27) becomes nickel (28).
e⁻Electron. Charge −1e. It is created at the moment of decay; it was not sitting inside the nucleus beforehand.
β⁻Beta particle. The name given to a high-speed electron emitted by a decaying nucleus. A beta particle and an electron are the same kind of particle; "beta" describes where it came from.
ν̄eElectron antineutrino. Neutral, almost massless, and barely interacts with matter. It carries away energy and momentum that would otherwise be unaccounted for.
β⁻ decayBeta-minus decay. The process in which a neutron becomes a proton and an electron plus an electron antineutrino are emitted. It is driven by the weak interaction.

Check the charge

Charge is conserved in every decay. Add up both sides of n → p + e⁻ + ν̄e in units of the elementary charge e.

ParticleSideCharge
NeutronBefore0
ProtonAfter+1
ElectronAfter−1
AntineutrinoAfter0
Total after0

0 = (+1) + (−1) + 0

The left side is a single neutron: total charge 0. The right side is a proton at +1, an electron at −1, and a neutral antineutrino at 0. They sum to zero, so charge balances exactly.

This matters for the experiment because it is one of the things that stayed reassuringly normal. Parity turned out not to be conserved, but charge, energy, momentum and angular momentum all were. The weak interaction broke one symmetry, not all of them.

What Wu found

With the cobalt-60 cooled and the nuclei lined up, the counting began. If parity were conserved, the electrons would have to come out with no preferred direction relative to the nuclear spin: as many along the spin axis as against it.

That is not what happened. The electrons were preferentially emitted opposite to the direction of the nuclear spin. The effect was large, it reversed when the field direction was reversed, and it faded away as the sample warmed up and the nuclei lost their alignment, exactly the behaviour expected if the asymmetry was genuinely tied to the nuclear spin rather than to some flaw in the apparatus (Wu et al., 1957).

The result arrived at the end of December 1956. It was checked, repeated, and published in Physical Review on 15 February 1957 under the title Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay (Wu et al., 1957). Parity is not conserved in the weak interaction.

Why the cooling was the hard part

A magnetic field can line up nuclear spins, but heat constantly knocks them out of line. At room temperature the thermal jostling wins completely and the nuclei point every which way, so any directional effect averages out to nothing. Only by getting to around a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero could the alignment survive long enough to count electrons. Wu's team had a window of a few minutes per run before the sample warmed and the effect disappeared.

Put the experiment in front of a mirror

On the left is what Wu actually saw. Reflect it, and ask yourself whether nature would ever produce the picture on the right.

The experiment as it happens
OBSERVED IN THE LABORATORY

The nuclear spin points up. Most electrons come out downwards, against the spin.

The same experiment, reflected
WHAT A MIRROR WOULD SHOW

The spin still points up, but now most electrons come out upwards, along the spin. Nature never does this.

Reflect the experiment and compare the two pictures.

Because spin is a rotation, not a direction of travel. Reflect the experiment top-to-bottom and the electrons, which are genuinely moving from one place to another, get their direction of travel reversed. The spin arrow is different: it is a bookkeeping arrow that stands for "the nucleus is turning this way", set by the right-hand rule. A top-to-bottom reflection leaves that turning sense unchanged, so the spin arrow is unaffected.

This is the whole trick. Quantities that behave like the electron's motion and quantities that behave like the spin respond differently to a mirror, so comparing them gives you a way to tell a real experiment from its reflection.

If both pictures happened equally often, you could be shown one of them with no labels and have no way to work out whether you were looking at the world or its reflection. That was the expectation: nature has no preference, and "left" and "right" are just names we assign.

Wu's result removed that. Because the electrons come out against the spin and not along it, the two pictures are physically different situations, and only one of them occurs. You can now define left and right using nothing but an experiment. You could describe the procedure to someone who has never met you and they would arrive at the same handedness. The weak interaction distinguishes them.

The sentence to carry out of this room

Wu's experiment showed that the weak interaction does not always behave the same way in a mirror image. Before her measurement, physicists took it for granted that nature cannot tell left from right. After it, they knew nature can.

ROOM 03 · THE ROAD WASN'T EQUAL

The Road Wasn't Equal

Wu's scientific record speaks for itself. The conditions she worked under are a separate story, and worth telling accurately: this room sets out what is documented about the barriers she met, the 1957 Nobel Prize, and the recognition that came later, without guessing at anyone's motives.

Two things at once

Wu was a woman in a field that was almost entirely male, and she was a Chinese immigrant in a country whose laws had explicitly restricted Chinese immigration for decades. Neither fact is incidental to her career.

When she arrived in 1936, the Chinese Exclusion Act was still in force; it was repealed in 1943, and even then the annual immigration quota for people of Chinese origin was set at roughly one hundred people. Wu became a United States citizen in 1954 (National Park Service, 2022), eighteen years after she arrived, and two years before the cobalt-60 experiment. For much of her career she was one of very few Chinese scientists in American physics, working through a period that included the Second World War and the Cold War, when scientists with ties to China faced particular suspicion.

At the same time, the professional world of physics assumed men. Women were routinely steered toward teaching positions at women's colleges rather than research posts at major universities, and were paid less when they held the same rank.

Barrier and achievement, in pairs

Each obstacle on the left is matched with what Wu did anyway. Open a row to read the detail.

Turned away from a graduate school entrance

Wu originally intended to study at the University of Michigan. She learned that women there were not permitted to use the main entrance of the student union building.

She went to Berkeley instead

She enrolled at the University of California, Berkeley, at the time one of the world's leading centres for nuclear physics, and completed her PhD there in 1940.

Restrictions like this were ordinary rather than exceptional. They were not usually framed as bans on women doing physics; they were small administrative rules about rooms, entrances, accommodation and membership that added up to a clear message about who a university was for. Wu's response, which was to choose the institution where the science was strongest and the rules were fewer, is a pattern that repeats through her career.

No research faculty post after her doctorate

Despite an outstanding record at Berkeley, Wu was not offered a faculty position at a major research university when she finished in 1940. Women in physics at the time were largely hired by women's colleges, if at all.

She built a research career anyway

She taught at Smith College, then became the first woman on the physics faculty at Princeton, and in 1944 joined Columbia, where she would stay for the rest of her working life and do her most important work.

Unequal pay at the same rank

Wu had been a full professor at Columbia since 1958 and held a named chair from 1973. Her salary was brought into line with that of male colleagues at equivalent rank in 1975 (National Park Service, 2022).

She spoke publicly about it

Wu used her platform to argue that women were not absent from science by inclination but by obstruction, and she pressed universities and professional bodies to change how they recruited and promoted.

Science is a collective activity, and how credit gets distributed within it is a recurring problem rather than a solved one. Large experiments involve theorists, experimentalists, technicians and engineers, while the most visible prizes usually name one to three individuals. Historians of science have documented a general pattern in which contributions by women have often been recorded less prominently than comparable contributions by men.

Wu's case is frequently cited in that discussion. What can be stated without speculation is straightforward: the experiment that tested Lee and Yang's proposal was designed and led by Wu and carried out with the low-temperature group at the National Bureau of Standards, and the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Lee and Yang.

The 1957 Nobel Prize

Set out plainly, with no claims about anyone's reasoning.

What Lee and Yang did

Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang reviewed the experimental literature in 1956 and showed that parity conservation had never been tested for the weak interaction. They proposed specific experiments that could test it. They received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics for this theoretical work (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, n.d.).

What Wu did

Wu designed and led the experiment that carried out the test. Working with Ernest Ambler, Raymond Hayward, Dale Hoppes and Ralph Hudson at the National Bureau of Standards, she produced the experimental evidence that parity is violated in beta decay, published in Physical Review in February 1957 (Wu et al., 1957).

What happened with the prize

Wu was not included as a Nobel laureate (National Park Service, n.d.). That is the documented fact. This exhibit does not attempt to explain why, because the deliberations behind the award are not something this project can establish. As general context, the statutes of the Nobel Prize limit a single prize to a maximum of three laureates.

The reaction within physics is documented. According to the National Park Service, Lee and Yang themselves sought to have Wu nominated for future prizes, and by 1966 she had received at least seven Nobel nominations (National Park Service, n.d.). She never received the prize.

She did receive the inaugural Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978, which the same source connects directly to her role in the discovery. The Wolf Prize has no three-laureate limit and is often awarded to scientists whose work is regarded as Nobel-calibre.

If you want to weigh this yourself, the right starting point is the primary source in Room 06: the 1957 paper lists the authors, and the National Women's History Museum and National Park Service biographies both describe the relationship between the theoretical proposal and the experimental test.

Recognition, eventually

Wu received a long list of honours during her lifetime. Select an entry to read about it.

Election to the National Academy of Sciences is among the highest professional honours available to a scientist in the United States. Wu was elected the year after the parity paper, and was also promoted to full professor at Columbia in the same year. She received an honorary doctorate of science from Princeton in 1958, the first woman to be awarded one there.

Columbia appointed Wu to a named chair, the first holder of the Michael I. Pupin Professorship of Physics. Named chairs are reserved for a university's most distinguished faculty.

The highest scientific honour conferred by the United States government, presented for outstanding contributions to knowledge. In the same year Wu received the American Physical Society's Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics.

The American Physical Society is the main professional body for physicists in the United States. Wu was elected its first woman president. Some sources date her term of office to 1975 and others to 1976, but the fact of the election, and that she was the first, is not in dispute.

Wu received the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978, the first time the prize was awarded in physics, making her its inaugural recipient. The Wolf Prize is regarded as one of the most significant international awards in the sciences.

ROOM 04 · PHYSICS CHANGED BECAUSE OF WU

Physics Changed Because of Wu

One measurement, taken over a few winter weeks in a basement laboratory in Washington, forced physicists to rebuild part of their picture of how the universe works. Follow the chain from the first doubt to the finished consequence. Every link opens.

The chain of discovery

Select any link to read what happened at that stage.

By the mid-1950s particle physicists had an awkward result on their hands: two particles then called tau and theta looked identical in every measurable property, yet decayed into final states of opposite parity. Either there were two nearly indistinguishable particles, or parity was not being conserved in the decay. The puzzle did not go away, and it forced physicists to ask an uncomfortable question about an assumption nobody had examined.

Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang worked through the published experimental record in 1956 and found something startling. Parity conservation had been demonstrated for the electromagnetic and strong interactions, but for the weak interaction the data simply did not settle the question either way. It had been carried along as an assumption. They published this, and set out concrete experiments that could decide it, one of which involved measuring the direction of electrons from aligned radioactive nuclei (Lee & Yang, 1956).

Wu was the obvious person to ask: she was the leading experimental authority on beta decay. She recognised immediately how important the measurement would be, cancelled a planned trip abroad, and set to work. Because no single laboratory had both a beta-decay setup and the ability to reach thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, she partnered with the low-temperature group at the National Bureau of Standards: Ernest Ambler, Raymond Hayward, Dale Hoppes and Ralph Hudson. Getting the apparatus to work took months of failures.

At the end of December 1956 the counts came in. With the cobalt-60 nuclei aligned, the electrons were not emitted evenly: noticeably more came out opposite to the direction of the nuclear spin than along it. The team then did what good experimentalists do: they reversed the magnetic field and watched the asymmetry reverse, and they let the sample warm and watched the effect disappear as the alignment was lost. The signal was real and it was tied to the spin.

An asymmetry like this cannot exist if parity is conserved. Published in Physical Review on 15 February 1957, the result showed that the weak interaction distinguishes between a process and its mirror image. Within weeks, colleagues at Columbia had confirmed parity violation in a completely different system, the decay of muons (Garwin et al., 1957), which removed any doubt that the finding was a quirk of cobalt-60.

Theorists had to rewrite the weak interaction so that handedness was built into it from the start, rather than treating mirror symmetry as automatic. The resulting description, in which the weak force couples to particles differently depending on their handedness, is fundamentally different from the theories of electromagnetism and the strong force, and it is a permanent feature of physics today. The discovery also opened the question of whether other symmetries could fail, which led directly to the study of combined charge-parity symmetry in the 1960s.

The modern account of fundamental particles and forces is called the Standard Model, and the weak interaction's handedness is written into it. The National Park Service's biography of Wu states that her experiment proved Lee and Yang's theories correct and contributed significantly to particle physics and the development of the Standard Model (National Park Service, n.d.). A measurement that began as a check on an untested assumption ended up as one of the foundations of the framework physicists still use.

A handed weak force had to be written into theory properly. The electroweak theory that followed predicted two heavy particles, the W and Z bosons, and finding them meant building accelerators and detectors on a scale physics had not attempted before. They were found at CERN in 1983. The detectors counted particles using scintillators and photomultiplier tubes, the same technology as Wu's counter, scaled up enormously.

Scintillator-and-photomultiplier detection is now how PET scanners and gamma cameras work in hospitals. Separately, cobalt-60, the isotope Wu used as a beta source, is the gamma source inside radiotherapy machines. The world's first cobalt-60 cancer treatment was given at Victoria Hospital in London, Ontario, on 27 October 1951 (Parks Canada, n.d.). Note the date: that is five years before Wu's experiment, so it was not caused by her work. It is the same isotope, used for something else.

Cobalt-60 units remain the main radiotherapy machine across much of the world, and detector physics underpins modern medical imaging. Understanding the weak interaction also explains why the Sun shines at all: the first step of fusion in the Sun is a weak-interaction process, so stellar lifetimes depend on the force Wu was probing. And her exclusion from the 1957 Nobel Prize became one of the most cited cases in arguments about who gets credited in science.

Before Wu, after Wu

What physicists could say about mirror symmetry on either side of February 1957.

Before
UP TO 1956
  • Parity conservation was treated as a universal law, holding for every fundamental interaction.
  • It had been tested and confirmed for the electromagnetic interaction and the strong nuclear interaction.
  • For the weak interaction it had never been tested, and the assumption was carried across without evidence.
  • "Left" and "right" were considered pure convention: no experiment could define them without reference to something external.
  • The tau-theta puzzle sat unexplained, with no accepted resolution.
  • The weak interaction was described by theories that assumed mirror symmetry.
After
FROM 1957
  • Parity is violated by the weak interaction. It remains valid for the electromagnetic and strong interactions.
  • The violation was confirmed independently in muon decay within weeks of Wu's publication.
  • "Left" and "right" can be defined by experiment: a measurement of beta decay distinguishes them.
  • The tau-theta puzzle dissolved: they are the same particle, decaying by a parity-violating interaction.
  • Theories of the weak interaction were rebuilt with handedness as a basic ingredient.
  • Physicists began testing other symmetries they had also assumed, leading to work on charge-parity symmetry.

If Wu's experiment had never happened…

A fair question with an honest answer.

It is impossible to know exactly what would have happened. What can be said is that Lee and Yang had published their proposal, so the question was in the open literature and other groups could act on it. Other experiments might eventually have provided evidence for parity violation, and the muon-decay measurements that followed Wu's result within weeks are a reasonable indication that the physics was within reach of more than one laboratory.

But "might eventually" is doing real work in that sentence. Nobody had acted on the question before Wu did, and most physicists thought the experiment was not worth the effort.

Timing in physics is not a detail. The late 1950s and 1960s were when the modern theory of particles and forces took shape, and parity violation arrived early enough to be built into that work from the beginning rather than bolted on afterwards. A delay of several years would have meant theorists developing their ideas on the assumption of mirror symmetry for longer. Whether the end result would have looked the same is not something anyone can state with confidence. The honest answer is that the development of particle physics could have unfolded differently.

Watch how this exhibit is worded

Notice that nothing above says "physics would have been set back twenty years" or "nobody else could have done it." Those claims feel satisfying and cannot be supported. A museum that invents a counterfactual to make its subject look bigger is doing her a disservice: Wu's actual, documented achievement is already substantial.

The documented claim

Wu designed and led the experiment that first demonstrated parity violation in the weak interaction, published in February 1957. The result changed how the weak interaction is described and contributed to the framework that became the Standard Model.

Reading about an experiment and running one are different things. In this room you assemble the apparatus yourself, emit the electrons, predict what a mirror would show, and then say the whole discovery back in your own words. Nothing here is decorative. Each interaction is doing a job.

Emit electrons and watch where they go. Switch between what parity conservation predicted and what Wu actually measured.

Pick a mode and emit some electrons.

How to read this

In the parity-conserving mode the two counters wander around each other and neither pulls ahead: with enough decays they settle near a 50-50 split. That is what "nature has no preferred direction" looks like in data.

In Wu's mode one counter runs clearly ahead and stays ahead, and it keeps doing so however many times you run it. That persistence is the whole result. A one-off fluctuation proves nothing, but a bias that survives repetition does.

This simulator is illustrative. It is built to show the shape of the result, an even split versus a clear preference, and the numbers it produces are not the measured values from the 1957 paper. For those, read the primary source listed in Room 06.

Q1If parity were conserved, what would you expect when the experiment is viewed in a mirror?

Q2Wu reversed the direction of the magnetic field partway through and the asymmetry reversed with it. Why did that matter?

Why I find her inspiring

What gets me about Wu is not that she was brilliant, though she was. It is that she was told, in a hundred small administrative ways, that physics was not really for her, and she kept choosing the harder room anyway. She picked Berkeley over a university that would not let women through the front door. She took on an experiment her own colleagues thought was a waste of nine months.

The part I keep coming back to is that she tried to destroy her own result. She reversed the magnetic field to see whether the effect would vanish. She let the sample warm up to check that the signal died with the alignment. She had the biggest finding of her career in hand and her instinct was to attack it. I find that harder to imitate than the cleverness, and more worth imitating.

And she did not get the prize. She kept working for another twenty-four years anyway, and used the platform she did have to argue that women were missing from science because of obstruction, not inclination. Doing good work without the reward arriving is a real thing to admire, and it is the bit of her story I would want to remember if I forgot everything else.

The line I would keep

Speaking at MIT in 1964, Wu asked her audience whether the tiny atoms and nuclei, or the mathematical symbols, or the DNA molecules have any preference for either masculine or feminine treatment (National Park Service, 2022).

THE ONE THING TO REMEMBER

Wu's experiment showed that the weak interaction does not always behave the same way in a mirror image.

Everything else in this museum (the cryostat, the cobalt, the counters, the prize she did not receive) exists to support that one sentence. Before 1957 physicists believed nature could not tell left from right. Chien-Shiung Wu built the apparatus that proved it can.

Diagrams

Every diagram on this site other than the two credited images above (the interactive apparatus in Room 02, the mirror comparison, and the build-it-yourself apparatus in Room 05) was drawn as original vector artwork for this project. No credit is required for those, but they are listed here so it is clear which visuals are sourced and which are not.

How the photographs are stored

All seven photographs are embedded directly inside this HTML file rather than loaded from the internet.

That means the site works with no connection at all, whether on a school computer, a locked-down network, or a USB stick, and there is no separate image folder to lose. Each photograph was converted to greyscale and reduced in size so the whole museum stays under two megabytes. The links in the credits above go to the original full-resolution files on Wikimedia Commons, where the licence for each one can be checked.

A note on accuracy: no fact, date, award or quotation on this site has been included unless it appears in one of the sources above. Where sources disagree, for example on whether Wu's term as president of the American Physical Society is dated to 1975 or 1976, the disagreement is stated rather than resolved silently.

The Mirror Room

A digital museum on Chien-Shiung Wu and the discovery of parity violation, built as a Grade 11 physics project. Photographs are credited to their sources; all diagrams are original to this site.
